name: Veet depilatory cream

lead: Veet is a mass-market depilatory brand whose creams dissolve the hair shaft so it can be wiped off at the skin surface. People use it on arms, legs, chest or other areas for smooth skin within minutes, without a razor.

Thioglycolate salts in a high-pH base break the disulfide bonds in hair keratin, softening the shaft until it wipes away. The follicle is left intact, so hair regrows within days. No clinical trials of the creams were found.

paras: The cream is spread over the area, left for the time on the label, then wiped or rinsed off. Users repeat it every few days as hair grows back, and many use it as an alternative to shaving or waxing.
Irritation and chemical burns are possible with alkaline depilatories, and labels advise patch testing. A 2002 case series linked Veet wax strips, not creams, to allergic contact dermatitis.

chain: Hair wiped off at skin surface
angle.text: Users apply Veet to leave arms, legs, chest or other areas smooth within minutes, without a razor. The cream dissolves hair keratin so the hair wipes off at the surface. The smooth result is visible immediately and hair typically regrows within days.

lead: Veet is a brand of chemical depilatory products, mainly creams, lotions and gels, that remove body hair by dissolving the keratin of the hair shaft so it can be wiped off at the skin surface. It is owned by Reckitt Benckiser and traces its origin to a Canadian product sold under the name Neet from 1919.[1][2]

The active chemistry is the same family used across the depilatory category: thioglycolate salts in an alkaline base that break the disulfide bonds in keratin.[2][3] Because the hair is cut below the skin surface but the follicle is left intact, hair regrows; Wikipedia notes depilatories do not destroy the dermal papilla.[3]

No clinical trials of Veet creams for appearance outcomes are indexed. The published literature on the brand consists mainly of a dermatology report of allergic contact dermatitis linked to Veet wax-strip products, which are a different product type from the creams.[4]
infobox: Chemical depilatory (cream, lotion, gel; also wax strips)
Thioglycolate salts in an alkaline base
Legs, underarms, bikini line, face, men's body hair

paras: Veet products are sold as tube creams, jar lotions, gels, sprays and wax strips for legs, underarms, bikini line and face, with variants for sensitive or dry skin and for men.[1][2] Marketing materials describe application times of a few minutes before the dissolved hair is wiped away.[1]

According to the manufacturer, thioglycolic acid and potassium hydroxide react to form potassium thioglycolate, which breaks keratin's disulfide bonds and weakens the hair.[2] Depilatory creams in general contain roughly 5-6 percent calcium thioglycolate in a high-pH base, a mixture that hydrolyses hair but is also irritating to skin if left on too long.[3]

The product originated as Neet, trademarked in Canada by the Hannibal Pharmacal Company in 1918-1919, with a US trademark granted in 1922.[2] The Veet name was established in the UK in 1922, and Canada and the US continued to use Neet until 2002.[2] Reckitt & Colman acquired the trademark in 1990 according to Wikipedia, while Grokipedia gives a 1969 acquisition date; the two sources disagree.[1][2] A 2022 reformulation range, Veet Pure, is described by Grokipedia as using plant extracts to reduce irritation.[1]

A 2002 report in Contact Dermatitis described 33 cases of acute allergic contact dermatitis in France and Belgium linked to Veet epilating waxes and their accompanying tissue; some were severe enough to require hospitalisation or systemic corticosteroids, and sensitisation sometimes occurred after the first use.[4] The report concerned wax products rather than depilatory creams.
Product labels generally advise patch testing and keeping the cream off broken or irritated skin; such label guidance is attributed to manufacturers and is not an independent finding.

Early advertising presented Neet as a faster alternative to shaving.[2] Wikipedia records that a 2014 Veet advertising campaign drew criticism for portraying unshaven women as masculine, and that one ad was withdrawn after complaints it was homophobic and transphobic; a 2011 French promotional site was also removed after complaints.[2]
No studies found. The nearest published research is a 2002 case series of allergic reactions to Veet wax products, not a trial of the cream.[4]
